content.title: Artemis II launches from NASA's KSC, Florida: Astronauts off on moon mission
content.text: 8:19 pm ET April 1, 2026NASA Administrator gives updateBrooke EdwardsNASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has given a post launch update. There was an issue with the communication system between mission control and the Artemis II crew. Communication has been restored.The crew is doing well and safely in orbit.7:42 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II traffic around BrevardBrooke EdwardsArtemis II post launch crowds are dispersing onto Brevard roads. Liftoff is set for 6:35 p.m.6:16 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II launch holdingBrooke EdwardsThe count is holding at T-10 minutes as teams work through final issues.6:05 pm ET April 1, 2026NASA has cleared battery issueBrooke EdwardsNASA has stated the issue has been cleared! No further issues have been mentioned by NASA.5:57 pm ET April 1, 2026NASA Crew-12 watches Artemis II launchBrooke EdwardsThe NASA SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts are watching the Artemis II launch onboard the International Space Station.5:55 pm ET April 1, 2026What the Artemis II astronauts are eating in spaceBrooke EdwardsNASA has released a menu of what the astronauts will be snacking on during their 10-day journey around the moon. Items include a variety of drinks, carbs, fruits, and vegetables.As for energy to power through the flight objectives and science experiments, NASA has included a total of 43 servings of coffee for the four astronauts.5:52 pm ET April 1, 2026How fast will the Artemis II SLS rocket travel at launch?Brooke EdwardsJust before the crew reaches orbit at about 8.5 minutes past liftoff, SLS will be traveling over 17,000 mph. That’s 23 times faster than the speed of sound.5:43 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II launch is Orion's first crewed flightBrooke EdwardsThis launch marks the first crewed flight of the Orion spacecraft. It will be the seventh new vehicle NASA astronauts will fly. Previous include:MercuryGeminiApolloSpace ShuttleSpaceX DragonBoeing Starliner5:41 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II SLS engines will send the rocket soaringBrooke EdwardsOnce the engines — alongside the two solid rocket boosters —get SLS off the pad, the rocket goes soaring off into space at approximately 17,000 mph. That is 13 times the speed of sound and would get you from Los Angeles to New York in just 15 minutes.Yet it all starts six seconds before liftoff, giving the core stage’s RS-25 engines enough time to start before the solid rocket boosters. During those final seconds, the steam becomes visible as it shoots out from the core stage of the rocket at 9,600 miles per hour.And the temperature? Hot enough to melt steel.5:34 pm ET April 1, 2026Weather improved to 90% favorableBrooke EdwardsWhile NASA is tracking a battery issue, the weather has improved to 90% favorable.The countdown clock is still moving toward a possible launch at 6:24 p.m.5:31 pm ET April 1, 2026Familiar names at Artemis II launchBrooke EdwardsArizona Senator Mark Kelly, who is a former NASA astronaut, is at Kennedy Space Center to see humans launch to deep space for the first time in over 50 years.The FLORIDA TODAY Space Team has spotted multiple astronauts at the press site waiting to witness their colleagues make history.5:11 pm ET April 1, 2026Range is GOBrooke EdwardsCrews have cleared the launch range! No constraints are present. NASA is working toward a launch as soon as 6:24 p.m.4:57 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II work being done to clear rangeBrooke EdwardsNASA has currently stated at the moment there is an issue with clearing the range − meaning the air space clearance to keep the public safe. If the range cannot be cleared, this would pose a delay to the launch.However, teams are working toward a resolution. All is still moving toward a launch attempt as soon as 6:24 p.m."Although the countdown to today’s Artemis II launch is continuing to progress, the Eastern Range has identified an issue that they are currently working to resolve related to their communication with the flight termination system," the NASA blog reads. "The flight termination system is a safety system that allows engineers on the ground to send a signal to destruct the rocket if it were to veer off course during ascent, to protect public safety. Without assurance that this system would work if needed, today’s launch would be no-go. However, engineers have devised a way to verify the system and are currently preparing to test this solution."4:47 pm ET April 1, 2026Brevard EOC active ahead of Artemis II launchBrooke EdwardsThe Brevard EOC has activated head of the upcoming Artemis II launch.4:42 pm ET April 1, 2026SLS’s engines have seen NASA space shuttle flightsBrooke EdwardsThe first engine has the title of Engine 2047. It flew on 15 shuttle missions. It first flew back in June 1998 on the Space Shuttle Discovery mission STS-91. The mission is known for the final docking of the Space Shuttle to the Russian space station Mir. These dockings paved the way for the collaboration to begin construction of the International Space Station in 1998, which has been continuously crewed since 2000.The second engine is engine 2059. It has five flights to its name.The third is engine 2061. It has seen two flights.The last, engine 2062, is seeing its first flight on Artemis II. While it was built and tested during the end of the shuttle era, it never got scheduled to fly before the shuttle retired in 2011.4:30 pm ET April 1, 2026The SLS rocket’s engines flew on the space shuttleBrooke EdwardsThe SLS rocket may only be flying for the second time, yet its core stage engines have flown to space multiple times.How is this possible?Meet the four RS-25 engines that will power the core stage of the SLS rocket. Built by L3 Harris, three of the four engines flew on NASA’s Space Shuttle fleet.4:19 pm ET April 1, 2026Astronaut: 'This is the launch of, I feel like, the decade'Rick NealeAstronaut Sian Proctor, who piloted the groundbreaking all-civilian SpaceX Inspiration4 orbital mission in September 2021, is at the Kennedy Space Center Press Site ahead of the Artemis II liftoff."It's huge. This is the launch of, I feel like, the decade — and I actually went to space a few years ago," Proctor said."Because I'm a moon celebration baby: I was born 8½ months after Neil Armstrong stepped foot on the moon. I feel like this is what my father's generation went through, because he was working at the NASA tracking stations during the Apollo missions," she said."And I can only imagine the excitement they all felt back then. And now, we have this whole new generation that gets to be inspired by Artemis and everything that we're doing," she said.4:07 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II astronauts will see 'dark side' of the moonBrooke EdwardsWhen the Artemis II Orion spacecraft flies around the far side of the moon, also known as the 'dark side', they will see views the Apollo missions did not. That is because the Apollo missions flew when the moon was in a different phase of lighting − the aim being the land the astronauts when the near side was illuminated.Congressman Mike Haridopolos laughed when Engagement Editor John A. Torres asked him if anyone snuck an 8-track cassette of the quintessential 70s Pink Floyd rock album onto Orion.“They’re gonna be by the dark side of the moon,” Haridopolos said with a smile. “We won’t hear from them for about 30 minutes (when that happens). I’ll get that 8-track ready, if nothing else I’ll pull it off of Apple iTunes.”On a more serious note, the congressman said “some of the new technology that will take place is that when they create satellites around the moon in just a few years, it will allow us to communicate with the dark side of the moon."−− John A. Torres3:45 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II moves toward launchBrooke EdwardsWhile watching no major issues, teams are watching possible weather constraints. The concern being upper winds, which would pose a danger if the spacecraft needed to abort. Weather is expected to move west, and out of the launch area.The Closeout Crew is working toward closing the outer hatch of the spacecraft − which is now pressurized.3:35 pm ET April 1, 2026Video of Artemis II astronaut drive byBrooke EdwardsSpace Reporter Brooke Edwards got this video of the Artemis II vehicle as it passed the press site on the way to the launch pad.3:21 pm ET April 1, 2026See photos of Artemis II astronaut walkoutBrooke EdwardsFLORIDA TODAY photographer Craig Bailey was at the crew walkout this afternoon. See photos of the astronauts as they leave the Operations and Checkout Building at Kennedy Space Center and head to the launch pad.3:13 pm ET April 1, 2026Closeout Crew preparing to close OrionBrooke EdwardsThe Closeout Crew is preparing to exit the Orion spacecraft and close the hatch. They will then leave the launch area − and if all goes well, in just over three hours the four astronauts will begin their journey around the moon.3:02 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II astronauts move through checksBrooke EdwardsThe Artemis II astronauts are strapped into Orion and moving through final checks before the hatch is closed.2:54 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II Orion spacecraft sits on top of SLS rocketBrooke EdwardsLooking at the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket it can be hard to tell where the spacecraft is situated. The Orion spacecraft is safely tucked away under the Launch Abort System – the white towering cover on top, which is designed to quickly pull the spacecraft away from the SLS rocket during an emergency.If that bad launch day were to happen, rocket motors on the tower pull, lift, separate, and steer the capsule into a safe parachute landing.Fully stacked, the Launch Abort System, Orion spacecraft and its service moduel underneath make up the top 67 ft of the SLS.The Orion spacecraft itself is approximately 11 feet tall and 16.5 feet in diameter. Orion has 12 thrusters, each with the ability to provide 160 pounds of thrust.Its mass at liftoff? A whopping 22,900 lbs with all its fuel. For reference, a pickup truck weighs between 4000 to 6000 pounds.As for the service moduel underneath, that provides the propulsion, thermal control, and life support systems. Its four solar arrays, which unfold in space, provide electrical power.It contains 24 thrusters, eight engines, and a main engine capable of 6,000 lbs. of thrust.2:40 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II astronaut rolesBrooke EdwardsAs the astronauts board the Orion spacecraft, here's the roles they will place in the spacecraft.Commander:Reid Wiseman will be responsible for communications with NASA mission control and among the astronauts.He is also responsible for assisting with controlling the Orion spacecraft.Pilot: Victor Glover is responsible for executing the maneuvers of the Orion spacecraft. He is named second in command.Mission Specialist 1:Christina Koch will be seated near the spacecraft’s hatch, taking on the role of hatch systems and operations. It will also be her role to set up the necessary toilet system once the crew is safely in orbit.Mission Specialist 2: Once the crew is safely in orbit, Jeremy Hansen will inspect the functioning of life support equipment inside Orion. He is also responsible for emergency equipment.2:22 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II Closeout CrewBrooke EdwardsThe Closeout Crew, the last people the astronauts see before liftoff, are getting the astronauts in Orion.As for what final words the Closeout Crew will say to the astronauts before the seal the hatch? That's a hard question.Hose and Warriner explained that the astronauts will likely not hear them after a certain point. With the communication system already on their ears, they'll be listening to launch control.“For the CDDT (countdown demonstration test), the only thing I was really able to get out for him, when we're closing the hatch was I just gave him a thumbs up as the door was going shut,” said Warriner.2:15 pm ET April 1, 2026Orion spacecraft softwareBrooke EdwardsWhile Lockheed Martin engineered the Orion spacecraft, local company, ENSCO, created the software for the cockpit display in the spacecraft. It’s called IData.The Artemis II crew will be the first astronauts to give feedback on ENSCO’s IData software, and will be able to give opinions on what worked well, what didn't and what could be improved. IData is in a reusable file which can see changes without having to undergo recertification – saving time before Artemis III takes off in 2027.“So this is the first one that's going to be manned, where they'll have somebody looking at the screen. And there will definitely be changes between (Artemis) two and (Artemis) three,” Bob Gillen, vice president of engineering at ENSCO told FLORIDA TODAY.ENSCO operates two offices on the Space Coast: one in Cocoa Beach and one in Melbourne. While the Melbourne facility focuses on work at nearby Patrick Space Force Base, the Cocoa Beach location focuses on work with both the Eastern Range and Western Range in California.1:51 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II astronauts head to launch padBrooke EdwardsReid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Chirstina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen have left the Operations and Checkout Buildings at Kennedy Space Center, and are off to the launch pad to board the spacecraft.1:33 pm ET April 1, 2026Amentum closeout Crew for Artemis IIBrooke EdwardsSporting white jumpsuits and an Artemis program truck, the Closeout Crew is responsible on launch day for getting the four astronauts into Orion and securing the spacecraft for launch.Along with them is one of the backup Artemis II crew members.“Our job is not over until that thing’s off the ground,” said Taylor Hose, Closeout Crew Lead.“So we can always have a scrub up until the SRBs go off,” said Hose. “And once the SRBs go off and we know the vehicle is good, the crew is good, and they're going to the moon.”1:31 pm ET April 1, 2026“Rise” the Artemis II zero-g indicatorBrooke EdwardsFlying with the crew will be a zero-g indicator, a plush moon with an Earth styled hat named "Rise," which will give a visual confirmation when the crew arrives in orbit and first experiences microgravity.Rise will also be carrying a microSD card with the names of all members of the public who submitted their names to fly on the Artemis II mission.Rise was created by a second-grade student in California and was selected out of submissions from more than 50 countries. The design was inspired by the iconic "Earthrise" photo taken by the Apollo 8 crew from lunar orbit.1:18 pm ET April 1, 2026Jeremy HansenBrooke EdwardsRole:Mission SpecialistHometown:Ailsa Craig, OntarioSpaceflight experience:Selected as a Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut in 2009, Artemis II will be his first spaceflight.1:09 pm ET April 1, 2026Artemis II astronauts suit up for the moonBrooke EdwardsThe Artemis II astronauts are suiting up for launch.
